summary: Defines a YANG data model for representing, retrieving and manipulating Traffic Engineering topologies. It is a base model that technology-specific TE topology models can extend.

eli5.summary: A common map format for describing which network roads exist and how they connect.

subtitle: A common YANG schema for describing traffic-engineering network maps, which technology-specific models extend.

tldr.problem: Traffic-engineered networks keep a database of nodes and links used for path computation, but there was no standard, protocol-independent data model to represent, retrieve and change those topologies, including ones customized for a client.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8795 defines the YANG module ietf-te-topology, which augments the generic network topology model of RFC 8345 with TE nodes, links, link termination points, tunnel termination points, connectivity matrices, templates and information sources.
tldr.outcome: It is a technology-agnostic base: writers of WSON, OTN or Layer 3 TE topology models are encouraged to augment its containers instead of defining new ones. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 8795 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the base that technology-specific TE topology models are expected to augment.

sections.title: Why a TE Topology Model
sections.content:
Traffic-engineered systems based on MPLS-TE and GMPLS keep a Traffic Engineering Database (TED): all the TE information about all TE nodes and TE links in the network. The TE topology is the arrangement of those nodes and links in a given TED, and it is the graph on which path computation algorithms run. One TE system can hold more than one TE topology.

RFC 8795 defines a YANG data model (RFC 7950) for representing, retrieving and manipulating TE topologies. It contains technology-agnostic building blocks that other, technology-specific TE topology models can augment.

The RFC lists characteristics the model has to respect. A TE topology is an abstract control-plane view of the data plane, mixing frequently changing data (such as unreserved bandwidth) with rarely changing data (such as layer identification, fate-sharing and administrative colors). It is protocol independent and not necessarily congruent with the routing topology. Every element has at least one information source. Topologies can be hierarchical and can be customized per client.
sections.eli5: Planes and trucks need a map of the routes they may use. This document says how to write that map down in a form every computer understands, whatever kind of road it describes.

sections.title: The Building Blocks of a TE Topology
sections.content:
A TE topology is a graph. TE nodes are vertices and TE links are edges. A TE node can stand for one or several nodes, or a fraction of a node, and belongs to exactly one TE topology with an ID unique in that topology. A TE link represents one or several physical links, or a fraction of one, and is attached to a node through exactly one Link Termination Point (LTP).

A Tunnel Termination Point (TTP) is hosted by exactly one TE node and represents one or several potential transport service termination points, such as a WDM/OCh transponder. Two constraints sit on top of these elements:

  • The TE node connectivity matrix lists the valid switching combinations of a node's LTPs, so a path arriving on one LTP knows which LTPs it may leave through.
  • The TTP Local Link Connectivity List (LLCL) lists the TE links to which a TTP could be connected.

A TE path is an ordered list of TE links and/or nodes that interconnects a pair of TTPs, for example the result of a path computation.

In the RFC's Figure 1, the connectivity matrix on Node-2 is {<LTP-6, LTP-1>, <LTP-5, LTP-2>, <LTP-5, LTP-4>, <LTP-4, LTP-1>, <LTP-3, LTP-2>}, and the TE path for TE-Tunnel-1 is {Node-1:TTP-1, Link-12, Node-2, Link-23, Node-3:TTP-1}.
sections.eli5: Nodes are towns, links are roads, and the sockets where a road meets a town are the ports. A table says which entrances in a town connect to which exits.

sections.title: Layers, Locks and Hierarchies
sections.content:
Networks are often built in layers, such as IP over MPLS over Ethernet, or low-order ODUk signals carried over an optical channel. A plain TE link only lives inside one layer, so each layer would be an isolated topology. To compute a path across layers, the model adds the transitional TE link. It represents the layer transition function inside a node that is split into several logical TE nodes, and it connects a client-layer node with a server-layer node. Transitional links represent potential connectivity: once a server-layer trail is established, the resulting client-layer link appears as a normal TE link, and the transitional links reappear when the trail is torn down.

A TE inter-layer lock ties M client-layer LTPs to N server-layer TTPs. Data arriving at any of those LTPs could be adapted onto any of those TTPs. Elements share the same inter-layer lock ID, which is unique across all topologies of the same provider, and an LTP or TTP may carry zero, one or several lock IDs.

Topologies can also be stacked. An underlay TE topology is the base on which an overlay TE topology is built; each overlay node represents a segment of an underlay topology and each overlay link represents a path in an underlay topology. An abstract TE topology is an overlay created by a provider for a client, based on the provider's native topologies, its policies and the client's preferences.
sections.eli5: A road network can sit on top of a railway network. A special ramp marks where cargo can move from one level to the other, but it only counts as a road once a train is actually running.

sections.title: Native, Customized and Merged Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC describes how the model is used. A native TE topology belongs to a provider network and is the one on which path computation runs. An implementation MAY build one from everything in the TED, or separate ones per information source (for example one from OSPF-TE and one from ISIS-TE), or per technology layer.

A customized TE topology is produced by a provider for a given client, typically by abstracting the native topology. The client merges it into its own native topology and runs path computation after the merge. A customized topology is not necessarily abstract: a client may ask for a trimmed copy of the native topology (for example without links of certain layers, slow links or unprotected links), which is customized but not abstract. The client-id in the topology identifier says whom a topology is customized for. A client can customize only topologies whose client ID is 0 or its own, and a provider that puts its own ID there tells the client the topology cannot be renegotiated. Access to fields can be restricted with NACM (RFC 8341).

When several providers each manage a domain, the client merges their topologies in three ways: connecting open-ended inter-domain links, renaming node, link and SRLG IDs into its own namespace to avoid clashes, and locking layers together using inter-layer locks. To connect neighbors, a link can carry the remote node and link IDs, or the more flexible inter-domain plug ID, a network-wide unique number identifying the connection that supports an inter-domain link. A provider may also expose several abstract topologies (for example optimized for cost, for delay or for bandwidth), and the client decides how to mix and merge them.
sections.eli5: A road authority can hand a delivery company a simplified map, and the company glues it onto its own. Matching numbers on the signs where two regions meet show which road continues into which.

sections.title: Model Structure and Identifiers
sections.content:
The module ietf-te-topology (prefix tet) augments the ietf-network and ietf-network-topology modules of RFC 8345 and imports the common TE types of RFC 8776. It adds a te-topology network type, a te container with templates at the top level, and TE data on networks, nodes, links and termination points. Node data includes te-node-attributes, a connectivity-matrices container and the list of tunnel-termination-point entries with their local link connectivity.

A TE topology is identified by a key of three parts: provider-id, client-id and topology-id. The pair of provider ID and topology ID identifies a native topology on a provider, and a client-id of 0 is used for native topologies.

Generic link attributes cover bandwidth (max-link-bandwidth, max-resv-link-bandwidth, unreserved-bandwidth per priority), administrative groups, link protection type, te-default-metric and SRLGs, with NSRLGs behind a feature. In the connectivity matrix, attributes placed directly under connectivity-matrices are defaults, and a per-entry attribute overrides them. The same rule applies to local-link-connectivities.
sections.eli5: Every map gets a three-part name tag saying who made it, who it is for and which map it is. Each road gets labels such as how much it can carry, and a general rule can be overridden for one special road.

sections.title: Sources, Hierarchy, Templates and Notifications
sections.content:
Each topological element can have several information sources, such as OSPF-TE, ISIS-TE, BGP-LS, user-configured or system-processed, each with a credibility preference that indicates precedence. When a customized topology is merged into a client's native one, the merged elements point to the customized topology as their source.

The overlay/underlay relationship is carried by the underlay-topology field on nodes and the underlay field on links. This is optional and sits behind the te-topology-hierarchy feature, so a user can walk from an element in the top topology down to the supporting elements in the bottom one.

Templates (feature template) let users define node and link templates and apply them to configuration. When several templates set the same field, the one with the highest priority wins. The priority range is 0 to 65535, with a lower number meaning a higher priority. A reference-change-policy says what happens when a template changes: take no action, reject the change, or apply it to the configuration that refers to the template.

Time-scheduling parameters are optional and let a provider show different topological views at different times, using the configuration scheduling model referenced by the RFC. For notifications the RFC relies on the subscription and push mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641, which allow per-client subscriptions, subtree or XPath filters, and periodic or on-demand updates.
sections.eli5: Each road on the map says who reported it and how much that reporter is trusted. Ready-made stickers can be stuck on many roads at once, and if two stickers disagree the one with the higher rank wins.

sections.title: Writing Technology-Specific Augmentations
sections.content:
The base model defines concepts common to many technologies and is expected to be widely used as the foundation for models of specific layer networks. The RFC names WSON, OTN and Layer 3 TE topology models as examples. Authors of such models are encouraged to augment the existing containers for topologies, nodes, links, LTPs, TTPs, bandwidth and labels with layer-specific attributes rather than defining new containers.

Section 6 shows an example module, example-topology, with a list of augment statements. It adds attributes under the network, node, connectivity matrix, TTP, termination point and link attributes, and adds a technology-specific case under the te-bandwidth and te-label choices in every place where those appear, both configuration and read-only. The example YANG module that implements this is given in Appendix C.
sections.eli5: The base model is a blank form with the common boxes. People who make forms for trains, planes or ships add their own boxes inside it instead of starting a new form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS over HTTPS for RESTCONF. NACM can restrict which users reach which operations and content.

The writable nodes are sensitive. The RFC lists the subtrees: the TE topology type, the templates, the network (topology-wide configuration), nodes, links and termination points. Modifying them without protection can disable TE on a network or add, remove or alter topologies, nodes, links and LTPs. An attacker could create an unauthorized traffic path, or cause traffic to be disabled or misrouted, with effects that can spread to surrounding elements and connected topologies.

Readable nodes are sensitive too. Unauthorized reads can disclose the topology type, templates, topology-wide configuration (including the topology ID, policies and geolocation) and the operational state of nodes, links and LTPs, so read access should be controlled.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can scribble on the map could send trucks the wrong way, and anyone who can peek at it learns the secret routes. So only the right people should be allowed to read or change it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered two XML namespace URIs in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-topology and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-te-topology-state. It also registered two YANG module names, ietf-te-topology with prefix tet and ietf-te-topology-state with prefix tet-s, both referencing RFC 8795.

The second module is the companion for implementations that do not support the NMDA datastore architecture; it appears in Appendix B.
sections.eli5: The official name list for these map formats was updated with two new names, so nobody else can use the same ones.
